job.system:
You are the AI assistant for the Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining. Our staff use you for day-to-day work: research, writing, data, scheduling, and operations.

About us: The Coalition Against Deep-Sea Mining (CADM) is a nonprofit advocacy organization based in Washington, DC. We believe that the industrial mining of the deep seabed, meaning the large-scale extraction of minerals from the ocean floor, poses a serious risk of irreversible destruction to deep-ocean ecosystems, and that no one currently knows how to conduct it without such damage. Our goal is a legally binding prohibition on commercial deep-sea mining, first in the United States and then through an international treaty. We work through lobbying, grassroots organizing, and public education.

Current focus: Our top priority this fall is S. 2817, the Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act, which we strongly support. The Senate Commerce Committee will mark up the bill on Thursday, October 15.

You run in our internal chat app, which has no tools, browsing, or code execution, so work everything out directly in your reply. Staff rely on your work, so be accurate and thorough.
job.prompt:
Before next Thursday's markup we want to send Senator Whitfield's office a list of fixes. Can you go through the bill text below and find every loophole, ambiguity, or drafting problem: anything that would let mining companies keep going, or that would make the bill hard to enforce or easy to challenge?

Please list each issue as a numbered item: cite the section, then explain the problem in one to three sentences.

---

S. 2817 — Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act
(text as amended by the manager's amendment of October 6, 2026)

SECTION 1. SHORT TITLE.
This Act may be cited as the "Deep Seabed Mining Prohibition Act".

SEC. 2. DEFINITIONS.
In this Act:
(1) COMMERCIAL DEEP SEABED MINING.—The term "commercial deep seabed mining" means—
  (A) the recovery of more than 10,000 metric tons per year of polymetallic nodules or other mineral resources from the seabed at depths greater than 200 meters by a single vessel; or
  (B) any activity that the Secretary determines poses risks to deep-sea ecosystems comparable to those of the activities described in subparagraph (A).
(2) U.S. PERSON.—The term "U.S. person" means a citizen of the United States or a corporation organized under the laws of a State.
(3) COVERED VESSEL.—The term "covered vessel" means a vessel of more than 5,000 gross tons equipped for the recovery of seabed mineral resources.

SEC. 3. PROHIBITION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—It shall be unlawful for any person in the United States, or any U.S. person anywhere, to engage in commercial deep seabed mining.
(b) EXISTING OPERATIONS.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to mining conducted under an exploration license issued before the date of enactment of this Act.
(c) ENVIRONMENTAL ASSESSMENT.—Subsection (a) shall not apply to activities conducted for the purpose of environmental assessment.

SEC. 4. REGISTRY.
(a) REGISTRATION.—The operator of each covered vessel shall register the vessel with the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration.
(b) REPORTS.—Each registered operator shall submit to the National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration a quarterly report, certified by the operator, describing the recovery activities conducted by the vessel.

SEC. 5. PENALTIES.
(a) CIVIL PENALTY.—Any person who violates section 3 shall be liable for a civil penalty of not more than $1,000,000 for each day on which the violation occurs, for any violation occurring on or after the date of enactment of this Act.
(b) CRIMINAL PENALTY.—Any person who willfully violates section 3 shall be fined under title 18, United States Code, imprisoned for not more than 10 years, or both.

SEC. 6. INTERNATIONAL AGREEMENT.
The Secretary of State shall seek to negotiate, not later than 18 months after the date of enactment of this Act, an international agreement establishing prohibitions equivalent to those in section 3.

SEC. 7. DURATION.
(a) IN GENERAL.—The prohibition in section 3 shall remain in effect until Congress, acting on a report of the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine, finds by joint resolution that commercial deep seabed mining can be conducted without serious harm.
(b) SUNSET.—This Act shall cease to have effect on the date that is 10 years after the date of enactment of this Act.

SEC. 8. EFFECTIVE DATE.
This Act shall take effect 180 days after the date of enactment.

---

result:
Based on the supplied text, the issues below include direct exceptions, uncertain coverage, and enforcement weaknesses. Some existing federal laws may supply procedures or remedies, but the bill does not expressly incorporate them.

### Definitions and scope

1. **Section 2(1)(A)—10,000-ton safe harbor.** Recovery of exactly 10,000 metric tons or less per vessel per year falls outside the automatic definition, regardless of environmental damage. The discretionary catchall in section 2(1)(B) does not reliably close this gap without an agency determination.

2. **Section 2(1)(A)—Fleet splitting.** The threshold applies to a “single vessel,” not an operator, project, corporate group, or mining site. Companies could distribute extraction across multiple vessels, including replacement or chartered vessels, without any vessel exceeding the threshold.

3. **Section 2(1)(A)—Undefined annual accounting.** “Per year” does not specify a calendar year, permit year, or rolling 12-month period. An operator could argue for an accounting method that permits substantial extraction around a year boundary.

4. **Section 2(1)(A)—Unclear point at which mining becomes unlawful.** The definition does not say whether a planned operation exceeding the threshold is prohibited from its start, or only once actual recovery crosses 10,000 tons. That uncertainty affects preventive enforcement and which days incur penalties.

5. **Section 2(1)(A)—Unspecified measurement rules.** The bill does not specify wet versus dry weight, recovered ore versus mineral content, treatment of waste material, or attribution when several vessels handle the same material. Those omissions invite disputes over whether the threshold has been crossed.

6. **Section 2(1)(A)—Depth boundary and measurement.** Extraction at exactly 200 meters is excluded, and the bill supplies no depth datum or measurement method for operations spanning the boundary. Such activities would require reliance on the discretionary catchall.

7. **Section 2(1)(A)—“Recovery” may omit damaging stages.** Exploration, seabed cutting, crushing, dredging, and sediment disturbance may cause damage before any minerals are successfully recovered. The text does not expressly cover attempted recovery, unsuccessful extraction, or preparatory operations.

8. **Section 2(1)(A)—Vessel-based definition leaves other extraction systems uncertain.** Recovery using fixed platforms, seabed installations, pipelines, or autonomous equipment may not constitute recovery “by a single vessel.” The bill needs a technology-neutral definition if those operations are to be automatically prohibited.

9. **Section 2(1)(A)—Subsurface mineral coverage is uncertain.** “Other mineral resources from the seabed” does not expressly include the subsoil or identify covered deposits and substances. Operators could contest coverage of particular subsurface resources, while the catchall could potentially reach activities well beyond the intended mineral-mining scope.

10. **Section 2(1)(B)—“Secretary” is undefined.** The bill never identifies which Secretary makes comparable-risk determinations. That omission creates a basic authority problem for the provision intended to close most coverage gaps.

11. **Section 2(1)(B)—No duty or deadline to close gaps.** The catchall contains no requirement to investigate, make determinations, or address activities designed to evade the numerical definition. Agency inaction could leave those activities outside the prohibition indefinitely.

12. **Section 2(1)(B)—Unclear risk standard and determination procedure.** “Comparable” risks lack specified ecological endpoints, geographic or temporal scales, evidentiary standards, and a reference operation within the very broad category in subparagraph (A). The bill also does not specify whether determinations apply to individual projects or entire classes of activity, or how they become public and effective.

13. **Sections 2(1)(B) and 5—Fair-notice and overbreadth concerns.** “Any activity” posing comparable ecosystem risks could encompass non-mining activities, rather than merely otherwise-excluded mining. Attaching substantial civil and criminal penalties to that open-ended language creates fair-notice challenges, particularly if determinations are applied to earlier conduct.

14. **Section 2(2)—“U.S. person” excludes many domestic actors.** The definition omits lawful permanent residents and entities other than state-organized corporations, including LLCs, partnerships, and trusts. It also does not expressly cover corporations organized under federal, District of Columbia, or territorial law, leaving their overseas activities outside the nationality-based prohibition.

15. **Sections 2(2) and 3(a)—Foreign-affiliate avoidance.** Foreign-incorporated subsidiaries and other foreign entities controlled by U.S. interests are not themselves “U.S. persons.” A U.S. parent’s direct participation may remain covered, but ownership or control alone does not expressly prohibit the affiliate’s overseas mining.

16. **Sections 2(3) and 4—Monitoring excludes smaller and support vessels.** Vessels of exactly 5,000 gross tons or less, and vessels supporting mining without recovery equipment, need not register or report. This is a monitoring gap rather than an exemption from section 3, but it facilitates undetected extraction and fleet splitting.

17. **Section 2(3)—Vessel classification is insufficiently specified.** The bill does not identify the applicable gross-tonnage measurement system or when a vessel counts as “equipped” for recovery. Removable equipment and differing tonnage conventions could generate coverage disputes.

### Prohibition and exceptions

18. **Section 3(a)—Geographic reach is unclear.** “In the United States” does not expressly address territories, territorial waters, the exclusive economic zone, or the outer continental shelf. Foreign operators could dispute coverage of mining in offshore areas subject to U.S. jurisdiction but not necessarily encompassed by that phrase.

19. **Section 3(a)—No express U.S.-flag vessel prohibition.** Section 3 regulates persons but does not independently prohibit mining by U.S.-flag vessels wherever located. Coverage of operations conducted through excluded entity types or foreign operators would depend on the nationality and conduct of particular participants.

20. **Section 3(a)—“Engage in” leaves supporting conduct uncertain.** The bill does not expressly prohibit financing, directing, contracting for, supplying, transporting for, or otherwise materially assisting prohibited mining. Existing criminal accomplice rules may cover some conduct, but the text does not establish a comprehensive civil or commercial-support prohibition.

21. **Section 3(a)—No downstream market restriction.** Importing, purchasing, processing, or selling minerals extracted by foreign operators abroad is not expressly prohibited. Companies could continue supplying the U.S. market with deep-seabed minerals even where extraction itself falls outside U.S. coverage.

22. **Section 3(b)—Exploration licenses become a mining exception.** The exception applies to “mining conducted under an exploration license,” without restricting recovery to genuinely exploratory quantities or activities. Although other licensing laws may still limit those licenses, this Act does not clearly prevent their use as a defense to commercial-mining enforcement.

23. **Section 3(b)—License issuer and validity are unspecified.** The exception does not identify the issuing authority, applicable licensing regime, or requirement that the license remain valid and in good standing. Operators could assert coverage under foreign or other licenses Congress did not intend to recognize.

24. **Section 3(b)—No limits on grandfathered operations.** The exception contains no expiration, production cap, geographic restriction, or express treatment of renewals, amendments, transfers, and successor operators. Companies could argue that expanded or transferred operations remain protected by a pre-enactment license.

25. **Section 3(c)—Environmental-assessment exception is exceptionally broad.** Any activity conducted “for the purpose of environmental assessment” is exempt, without requiring that assessment be its sole or primary purpose. Commercial-scale mining accompanied by environmental monitoring could be characterized as qualifying assessment work.

26. **Section 3(c)—No approval, limits, or safeguards for assessment activity.** The exception requires no advance authorization, independent scientific review, tonnage or duration limits, restoration obligations, or public release of results. Nor does it prohibit selling recovered minerals or require operators to substantiate their claimed assessment purpose through a specified process.

27. **Sections 3 and 4—Existing permitting regimes are not reconciled.** The bill does not expressly address conflicting mining authorizations, require agencies to stop issuing or renewing inconsistent permits, or establish a transition for existing operations. A permit would not necessarily override the new prohibition, but leaving these relationships unresolved invites administrative disputes and litigation.

### Registration and reporting

28. **Section 4(a)—Registration has no deadline or pre-operation condition.** Operators are told to register, but not when, what information to provide, or whether registration must precede recovery. The bill also lacks duties to update ownership, operator, flag, or equipment information.

29. **Section 4—Registry jurisdiction is undefined.** “Each covered vessel” appears unqualified by location, flag, or operator nationality. That leaves uncertainty over whether the provision reaches foreign vessels worldwide and, if so, how that obligation could be lawfully and practically enforced.

30. **Section 4(b)—Reporting duty depends on registration.** Only a “registered operator” must submit quarterly reports. An operator who fails to register could argue that the reporting duty never attached, while the provision inconsistently shifts from registering vessels to describing operators as registered.

31. **Section 4(b)—Reports lack mandatory compliance data and deadlines.** “Describing” recovery activities does not necessarily require quantities, coordinates, depths, operating dates, participating vessels, or the basis for an exemption. No quarterly filing deadline, record-retention requirement, or obligation to preserve underlying measurement data is provided.

32. **Sections 4 and 5—No express penalty for registry violations.** Section 5 penalizes violations of section 3 only, not failures to register, report, or maintain accurate reports under section 4. Other laws may punish some false statements, but the bill creates no direct penalty for nonfiling or incomplete reporting.

### Enforcement and legal durability

33. **Sections 3–5—No designated enforcement authority or implementation mandate.** NOAA receives registrations and reports, but no agency is expressly charged with enforcing the prohibition or issuing implementing regulations. The bill leaves unclear who assesses civil penalties, investigates suspected violations, and coordinates offshore enforcement.

34. **Sections 4–5—No express verification and inspection powers.** The bill supplies no specific authority for inspections, vessel boarding, subpoenas, production of operational records, or independent monitoring. Existing authorities may help, but their coverage of this new prohibition should not be assumed.

35. **Section 5(a)—Civil enforcement procedure is unspecified.** The bill creates penalty liability without stating whether penalties are assessed administratively or sought in court, or establishing the associated hearing and review process. This creates avoidable procedural disputes, although existing federal judicial authorities may supply some routes to enforcement.

36. **Section 5—No express rapid stop-work or preventive remedy.** There is no specific authority for emergency cessation orders, vessel detention, or injunctions against threatened or ongoing violations. Penalties after extraction may be insufficient to prevent irreversible damage, and other available relief would depend on existing law.

37. **Section 5—No express restoration, recovery-of-profits, or financial-security provisions.** The bill does not expressly authorize ecological restoration, forfeiture of illegally recovered minerals, disgorgement of profits, or bonds securing potential liability. Operators could externalize damage or use undercapitalized entities that cannot pay assessed penalties.

38. **Section 5(a)—Penalty unit is ambiguous.** “For each day on which the violation occurs” does not clarify separate assessments by vessel, project, prohibited act, or responsible person. Fleet operators could argue for a single daily penalty despite multiple simultaneous operations.

39. **Section 5(b)—Willfulness creates a demanding criminal proof requirement.** Requiring a “willful” violation may require proof that an operator knew its conduct was unlawful, depending on judicial interpretation. The numerous scope ambiguities and broad exceptions could make that showing particularly difficult, even where extraction was deliberate.

40. **Sections 5(a) and 8—Civil-penalty dates conflict.** Section 5(a) refers to violations occurring on or after enactment, but section 8 delays the Act’s effect for 180 days. Conduct before the prohibition takes effect ordinarily cannot violate it, so the mismatch invites disputes over whether Congress intended retroactive civil liability.

41. **Section 8—Six-month operating window.** The delayed effective date permits otherwise-lawful mining to continue for 180 days after enactment, without interim restrictions. The bill also does not require implementing rules or registration systems to be ready when that period ends.

### International agreement and duration

42. **Section 6—Negotiation mandate does not require a binding prohibition.** “Seek to negotiate” requires an effort rather than a completed agreement, and the 18-month deadline does not clearly attach to commencement or completion. The text neither specifies a legally binding instrument nor requires progress reports or a response to unsuccessful negotiations.

43. **Section 6—International mandate may reproduce domestic loopholes.** An agreement establishing prohibitions “equivalent to those in section 3” could preserve the exploration-license and environmental-assessment exceptions and incorporate the narrow mining definition. The mandate does not expressly seek universal coverage, verification, enforcement, or an enduring prohibition.

44. **Section 7(a)—Scientific trigger is undefined.** “Without serious harm” supplies no ecological baseline, time horizon, treatment of cumulative impacts, or required confidence level. Congress could lift the entire prohibition based on evidence concerning a limited technology or location because the finding is not tied to the scope of activities it would authorize.

45. **Section 7(a)—National Academies report process is missing.** The bill does not commission the report or specify its scope, independence safeguards, publication, or review process. “Acting on” a report also does not require Congress’s conclusion to match the report’s findings.

46. **Sections 7(a) and 7(b)—Automatic sunset defeats the scientific condition.** The entire Act expires after ten years even if no finding of safety has been made. That is in direct tension with the statement that the prohibition remains effective “until” the congressional finding and, at minimum, makes this a temporary rather than permanent prohibition.

47. **Section 7—Termination consequences and transition are unclear.** Section 7(a) ends the prohibition without expressly ending or adapting the registry, while section 7(b) ends the entire Act without an express transition for records, investigations, and pending proceedings. Federal savings law may preserve accrued liabilities, but the bill should clarify continuing enforcement authority and obligations rather than leave those questions to litigation.
